latin: Mater familias<sup>1</sup> it obsonatum<sup>2</sup>. Apud lanium carnem emit bubulam (vitulinam, ovillam, suillam)<sup>3</sup>.
A pistore panem petit<sup>4</sup>. E pistrina exit. In macello olera<sup>5</sup> varia obsonat. In tabernam condimentariam intrat.
Condimentarius. — Salve, Domna! Quid petis?
Domna. — Opus est sale, pipere, lagona olei una, aceti litro uno, sacchari kilogrammate uno, ciceribus, faselis siccis, lentibus<sup>6</sup>.
C. — Quantum faselorum, quantum lentium?
D. — Faselorum kilogrammata duo, lentium sesquilibram<sup>7</sup> emam.
C. — Tibi dabo capsam in qua haec omnia collocare possis.
D. — Gratias! Da quoque farinam, pastas, oryzam.
C. — Haec nunc in sacculis praebentur: sacculos suppeditare mundius est quam grana e sacco manibus prehendere, et facilius quam lancibus<sup>8</sup> appendere<sup>9</sup>.
D. — Estne tibi sapo<sup>10</sup> ad munditiem<sup>11</sup> aptus?
C. — Hunc quoque, Domna, habeo. Ut sol nubes, sic sapo «Lunae Lux» sordes depellit<sup>12</sup>!
english: The mother [of the] family goes [shopping] (to do the errands). At the butcher's she buys beef (veal, mutton, pork).
At the baker's she asks for bread. She comes out of the bakery. At the market, she buys various vegetables. She goes into [the grocer's] (the grocer shop).
The grocer. — Hello Madam! What [would you like] (are you looking for)?
The lady. — [I need] (there is need of...) salt, pepper, a bottle of oil, a litre of vinegar, a kilo of sugar, chickpeas, dried beans, lentils.
G. — How many beans? How many lentils?
L. — Two kilos of beans, a pound and a half of lentils (I will buy).
G. — [I'll give] (I will give) you a box in which [you can] (subj.) put all that.
L. — Thank you! Give [me] also flour, pasta and rice.
G. — These things are now supplied in packets: supplying packets is cleaner than taking the grains [out of the] sack with one's hands, and easier than weighing them on the scales.
L. — [Do you have] toilet soap (is to you soap suited to cleanliness)?
G. — Madam, I have that too. Just as the sun [chases away] the clouds, «Moonlight» soap chases away dirt!

footnotes: Mater familias, pater familias (or familiae), plural matres familias (ae or arum), patres f... In this expression familias is not declined. But the expression keeps a regular form if familias is replaced by familiae (gen. sg. of familia, -ae), or familiarum (gen. pl.).
Obsonare (sometimes obsonari), to make provisions (of food), to buy (a narrower sense than emere).

The adjectives bubulus, -a, -um; vitulinus; etc.; correspond to the nouns: bos, bovis, m., (gen. pl. boum, dat. abl. pl. bobus or bubus); vitulus, -i, m.; ovis, -is, f., the ewe (the ram is called vervex, -ecis, m.); and sus, suis, m. (3rd decl.). For this last animal, one also says porcus, -i, m., noun to which the adjective porcinus corresponds.

Peto, -is, -ere, ivi or ii, itum, to seek to reach a place; to go and look for something, to claim. We saw this verb in the first sense (L. 10, P. 8). In the other two senses, one says petere aliquid ab aliquo, to ask something of someone (ablative), and not dative, since one is going to receive FROM someone and not give TO him something.
Macellum, -i, the market; olus, oleris, n., vegetable.

Oleum, acetum, saccharum, neuters of the 2nd declension; sal, salis, m., abl. sale; kilogramma, -atis, n., word of Greek origin (one should write, in accordance with Greek, chilo or even chilio, but the international symbol used for ×1000 is k. Although it is wrong, we have preferred to follow current usage). Finally piper, -eris; cicer, -eris; are neuters of the 3rd declension.
Sesqui, is a prefix that means: × 3/2. E.g.: sesquipedalis, a foot and a half long (3/2 foot); likewise semi, × 1/2; semipedalis, half a foot long.
Lanx, lancis, f., the dish; in the plural, lances, -ium, the scales (cf. L. 20, N. 3).

Pendo, -is, -ere, pependi, pensum, to weigh; a transitive and sometimes intransitive verb. E.g.: hic saccus 100 kg pendit, this sack weighs 100 kg. Appendo, -is, -ere, appendi, appensum, to weigh (less used, but always transitive); e.g. condimentarius cicera appendit, the grocer weighs the chickpeas.
Sapo, -onis, m., nubes, -is, f.; sordes, -ium, f. pl.; the latter gave the adjective sordidus, dirty, sordid.

Mundus, -a, -um, clean; comparative mundior, -ioris (neuter: mundius, same genitive); superlative mundissimus (not to be confused with mundus, -i, m., the world); opposite: immundus, dirty, filthy; munditiae, -ei, f., cleanliness, whence the toilet.
Pello, -is, -ere, pepuli, pulsum, to push; depello, -is, -ere, depuli, depulsum, to push away, to drive away.
comments: Today the exercise is a little long, but it is not difficult. As it contains a fairly abundant vocabulary, we do not ask you to try to retain it. Simply note the use of the FUTURE IMPERATIVE: sternito, ponito, etc. (see grammatical appendix). Note also the subjunctives spectet (so spectare); tangat (so tangere, 3rd conjugation); appareat (so apparere, 2nd conjugation) but also the future tangent.

But if you are courageous and still have a few minutes to spare, we do not forbid you to take a dictionary and look up the declension of the nouns and the principal tenses of the verbs about which you may have doubts. Thus you will find: dolium, -ii, n.; obruo, -is, -ere, -rui, -rutum, etc.

M. Porcius Cato (235-149 B.C.) supported the struggle against Carthage relentlessly. He wrote the De Agricultura, from which we give you this extract as an exercise. This shows you that the salting of hams does not date from yesterday!

latin: Cato, in libro De Agricultura, salsuram pernarum sic describit:
Pernas salire sic oportet in dolio aut in seria.
In fundo dolii aut seriae sale sternito, deinde pernam ponito...
cutis deorsum spectet; sale obruito totam.
Deinde alteram insuper ponito, eodem modo obruito.
Cave ne caro carnem tangat.
Ita omnes obruito.
Ubi jam omnes composueris, sale insuper obrue ne caro appareat: aequale facito.
Ubi jam dies quinque in sale fuerint, eximito omnes cum suo sale.
Quae tum summae fuerint, imas facito, eodemque modo obruito et componito.
Post dies omnino XII (pr. duodecim) pernas eximito et salem omnem detergeto spongia bene, perunguito oleo, suspendito in fumo biduum.
Tertio die demito, perunguito oleo et aceto commixto, suspendito in carnario.
Nec tinea nec vermes tangent.
english: Cato, in [his] book On Agriculture, describes the salting of hams thus:
[This is how] (thus) hams must be salted in a barrel or in a jar.
At the bottom of the barrel or the jar [spread] (imp. fut.) (you will have to spread with) salt, then put the ham...
let the skin [face] (look) downwards; [cover] (imp. fut.) it all with salt.
Then put another (ham) on top, cover it (imp. fut.) in the same way.
[Take care] (be careful) that the meat does not touch the meat.
Cover them (imp. fut.) all in the same way.
When you have [put them all in place] (you will have arranged them all), cover (imp. pres.) with salt on top so that the meat does not show: [level it out] (you will have to make it equal).
When they have [already] been in the salt for five days, take them out (imp. fut.) all with their salt.
Those that were on top (higher), put (imp. fut.) them underneath (you will have to make them lower); then cover and arrange (imp. fut.) them in the same way.

After twelve days in all, take out the hams (imp. fut.) and remove (imp. fut.) all the salt with a sponge, coat with oil, [put them to smoke for two days] (you will have to hang in the smoke for a space of two days).
The third day take them down (imp. fut.), coat with oil and vinegar mixed, hang (imp. fut.) in the larder.
Neither moth nor worms will [touch them].
